name: Spinach
description: Spinach at peak season exhibits tender, crisp leaves with a mild, slightly sweet earthy flavor. Spring spinach has delicate, smaller leaves ideal for raw salads, while fall spinach develops thicker, more robust leaves with deeper complexity after light frosts convert starches to sugars. Cold-acclimated fall spinach shows noticeably sweeter, less bitter character compared to warm-season commodity versions.

name: Asparagus
description: Fresh asparagus has a bright green color with a tender, crisp texture. The flavor is earthy and grassy with subtle sweetness and a mild nutty undertone. Peak-season spears snap cleanly when bent, have tightly closed tips with no ferning, and a fresh, herbaceous aroma with no bitterness or off-odors.

name: Rhubarb
description: Rhubarb delivers a sharp, tart bite from high malic and oxalic acid content, reminiscent of green apple with subtle celery undertones. Peak-season stalks are crisp and tender with bright red color and delicate flavor; summer rhubarb develops deeper red tones but stronger tartness and slightly woody texture. Freshly harvested stalks are glossy and firm.

name: Strawberries
description: Peak season Illinois and Michigan strawberries are deeply sweet with bright acidity, firm yet juicy texture, and pronounced floral aroma. Field-ripened berries develop full sugar complexity only in the 3–4 weeks between mid-May and mid-June. Commodity or early-season imports lack the depth and resilience of local, fully mature fruit.

name: Tart Cherries
description: Tart cherries deliver a bright, complex tartness with balanced acidity and subtle sweetness. The flavor is distinctly sour — twice as acidic as sweet cherries but with half the sugar content — yet carries fruity, almost citrus-like notes. Montmorency, the dominant variety, has yellow flesh with a vivid bright red skin and a pronounced tangy bite that makes them ideal for cooking and baking rather than fresh eating.

name: Blueberries
description: Fresh blueberries offer a bright balance of sweetness and gentle tartness with subtle floral and earthy undertones. Peak-season berries from Michigan's sandy glacial soils are plump and juicy with deep purple-black color and a natural powdery bloom coating. Michigan's Southwest region produces over 100 million pounds annually on soils and a lake climate that concentrate flavor in ways Illinois sandy loam cannot replicate at scale.

name: Raspberries
description: Peak-season raspberries are tender, juicy, and delicate with a bright sweet-tart balance and pronounced fruity-floral aroma. Summer-bearing varieties ripening July through August deliver intense flavor, while fall-bearing varieties extend availability into October with richer, jammier character. Fresh, locally grown raspberries possess superior flavor complexity and firmness compared to shipped commodity berries, which often arrive soft and diminished.

name: Plums
description: Peak-season plums deliver bright sweetness balanced by subtle tartness, with juicy, tender flesh and a delicate floral-fruity aroma. Japanese varieties are juicier with pronounced tartness ideal for fresh eating, while European plums offer sweeter, denser character with a subtle almond note from benzaldehyde compounds. Michigan and Illinois plums reach maximum sugar concentration and flavor complexity in mid-to-late summer.

name: Cantaloupe
description: Ripe cantaloupe offers a sweet, honey-like flavor with succulent, juicy flesh and a distinctive musky aroma. Locally grown Illinois and Midwest cantaloupes ripen fully on the vine, developing maximum natural sweetness that distant commodity melons picked immature never achieve. The Illinois River Valley's sandy soils and warm, humid summers enable vine-ripening that concentrates sugar and aroma in a way shipped fruit cannot match.

name: Zucchini
description: Zucchini has a mild, slightly sweet taste with subtle grassy and earthy notes. When young and tender at 6–8 inches, the flesh is delicate with soft seeds and a faint nutty flavor that intensifies when roasted. Oversized specimens become watery and bland; peak-season local zucchini from Illinois farms offers crisp texture and clean flavor at their best.

name: Heirloom Tomatoes
description: Heirloom tomatoes are open-pollinated varieties with complex, intensely sweet flavors derived from dramatically higher sugar levels than commercial cultivars. At peak season, they offer a juicy, almost buttery texture with variable flavor profiles by variety — Brandywine delivers rosy pink skin and intense tomato notes, while Cherokee Purple provides deep, smoky complexity. Their thin skins and fragile cell walls create exceptional flavor but make them prone to bruising.

name: Sweet Corn
description: Local sweet corn has markedly higher sugar content than grocery store corn because it's eaten within hours of picking, before sugars convert to starch. Illinois' fertile glacial soil and warm summer days amplify this effect — field-to-table timing matters more than variety. Early July ears are starchier; mid-July through August is peak with the sweetest, most tender kernels; September ears turn starchy again.

name: Watermelon
description: Peak-season watermelon delivers a crisp, juicy texture with bright, clean sweetness and subtle floral undertones. Illinois-grown melons reach maximum sugar content under long, hot summer days, developing significantly sweeter and more complex flavor compared to early-season or imported specimens harvested green. Look for a creamy yellow ground spot on the underside — white or pale green indicates underripeness — and a heavy weight relative to size.

name: Peach
description: Illinois peaches offer the quintessential summer stone fruit experience: tender, juicy flesh with a distinctive balance of sweetness and subtle tartness. Yellow varieties deliver the classic peach flavor with vibrant floral aroma, while white peaches provide a delicate, pure sugar-forward taste. Peak season peaches have fine-grained, succulent texture and a sweet, fruity fragrance that indicates full ripeness.

name: Concord Grapes
description: Concord grapes deliver a distinctive sweet-tart flavor defined by methyl anthranilate, the aromatic compound responsible for their signature musky, fruity character with notes of grape candy and subtle cherry. The flesh is succulent and gelatinous, contained within a thick, chewy slip-skin that easily separates from the fruit, creating a unique popping sensation. Southwest Michigan's Van Buren and Allegan counties produce over 7,400 acres of Concords — the largest juice grape concentration in the U.S. — where the lake climate develops full color and flavor that inland-grown berries don't achieve.

name: Apples
description: Illinois and Michigan apples reach peak flavor and sweetness as temperatures cool into fall. Early-ripening varieties like Gala and Honeycrisp appear in late August and early September with crisp, juicy flesh. Late-season varieties like Mutsu and Arkansas Black continue through November, developing deeper sweetness and complexity. At peak, quality apples are firm with no soft spots, smooth skin, and ground color that has shifted from green to yellow or golden.

name: Pumpkin
description: Peak-season pumpkins, especially sugar or pie varieties, are dense and sweet with earthy undertones. Sugar pumpkins (4–8 pounds) offer superior texture and flavor compared to larger carving varieties, with moist, thick flesh ideal for roasting, soups, and baking. Illinois leads the nation in pumpkin production — over 90% of U.S. canning pumpkins are grown here — meaning local supply is abundant and fresh through fall.

name: Pears
description: Peak-season pears, particularly Bartlett varieties from Illinois and Michigan, deliver a buttery, juicy texture with aromatic sweetness and subtle floral notes. Bartlett pears ripen off the vine at room temperature — they're picked firm and sweeten as they yellow, unlike most fruit that peaks on the plant. Ripe pears yield slightly at the stem end and emit a floral fragrance; underripe pears are crunchy and tart.

name: Cranberries
description: Peak-season fresh cranberries are bright red, firm, and juicy with a distinctive balance of sharp tartness, subtle sweetness, and an astringent puckering quality from natural tannins. Wisconsin produces approximately 65% of all U.S. cranberries — with Wood County alone growing roughly one in nine cranberries worldwide — and the cool autumn temperatures of harvest season develop the full anthocyanin color and flavor complexity that earlier or warmer-grown fruit lacks. Look for glossy, firm berries with deep red color; dull or soft specimens indicate age or bruising.
